match.reason: The bank point covers the 1967 referendum but is broader than the new point: it also teaches the 2023 Voice referendum, is written for Victorian Legal Studies, and does not state what the 1967 change did not grant, so it does not match the new point exactly.

draft.title: The 1967 referendum
card: A referendum is a national vote on a proposed change to the Constitution. In 1967, Australians voted on changes that affected First Nations Australians.
The first change let the Commonwealth Parliament make laws for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Before this, the states held that power.
The second change meant First Nations people were counted in the census, the official count of the population. Before this, they were left out of the national count.
Over 90 per cent of voters said Yes, one of the largest Yes votes in Australian history. The referendum did not itself grant citizenship or the vote.
draft.remember: The 1967 Yes vote gave the Commonwealth law-making power and a census count, not citizenship or the vote.

a.q: Which pair of results came from the 1967 referendum vote?
opts: Commonwealth law-making power and a census count
Citizenship and the right to vote nationwide
Return of land and an end to state laws
A treaty and a separate First Nations parliament
a.why: The Yes vote let the Commonwealth make laws for First Nations people and include them in the census. It did not itself grant citizenship or the vote, return land, or create a treaty.
a.clue: Think of the two changes put to voters: laws and the census.

b.q: Mia says the 1967 referendum gave Aboriginal people the vote in Australia. Why is she wrong?
opts: It gave the Commonwealth law-making power, not voting rights
It applied only to Torres Strait Islander people
Fewer than half of voters supported the change
It changed only the census and made no change to laws
b.why: The referendum changed the Constitution so the Commonwealth could make laws for First Nations people and count them in the census. It did not grant the vote. The last option is tempting, but the law-making change was one of the two changes.
b.clue: Recall what the Yes vote did and did not grant.

a.best: Commonwealth law-making power and a census count

b.best: It gave the Commonwealth law-making power, not voting rights

problems.detail: The clue 'Think of the two changes put to voters: laws and the census' names both parts of the right option, so students can match it without recalling the idea.

Why (b) says 'The last option is tempting', but options appear in random order, so this does not point to any fixed option. It also seems to describe the 'changed only the census' distractor while praising the law-making point, which is confusing.

'Before this, the states held that power' oversimplifies. The Commonwealth could already make laws for Aboriginal people in its territories, such as the Northern Territory. It was within the states that power lay with the states. Consider 'in the states, the states held that power'.

check.summary: The facts are sound and both questions have one clear answer. Question a's clue gives the answer away. Why (b) refers to 'the last option', which has no fixed meaning when options are shuffled. The card slightly oversimplifies who held the power before 1967.

proposal.title: The 1967 referendum
card: A referendum is a national vote on a proposed change to the Constitution. In 1967, Australians voted on changes that affected First Nations Australians.
The first change let the Commonwealth Parliament make laws for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the states. Before this, in the states, the states held that power.
The second change meant First Nations people were counted in the census, the official count of the population. Before this, the Constitution left them out of the official population totals.
Over 90 per cent of voters said Yes, the highest Yes vote of any Australian referendum. The referendum did not itself grant citizenship or the vote.
proposal.remember: The 1967 Yes vote gave the Commonwealth law-making power and a census count, not citizenship or the vote.
